job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Wendy Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I check the job boards on my phone before I get out of bed, because that's when the new postings go up. Then I send two or three applications from the desk in my rented room on Mill Road, which I share a house with my housemate Priya. Three days a week I do the till at the garden centre out by the ring road, and that pays for my rent and not much else. I graduated in accounting at Carrow University last summer, top of the class, with two internships, one at an audit firm and one in the finance team at the housing trust. Four months on, I've sent 63 applications and got eleven rejections and a lot of silence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say it changes nothing for people like me, so good. If it's mostly hype then the graduate schemes should come back to normal sooner or later. I'd tell my friends that the problem was never the robots, it was firms deciding to hire fewer juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still stuck. I have under a month of rent saved and 41,000 in student debt, and the nearest firms that hire trainee accountants are an hour's train away. Nothing about AI changes that, so I'm worried regardless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending ten applications a week and widen the search to the public sector and the charities. I'd also ask the housing trust whether their temporary cover roles could turn into something. I'd keep the garden centre shifts and cut the train trips to interviews to only the ones that really matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit heavy, to be honest. I'm calm about the technology, but I'm tired. Every week without an offer the debt statement feels louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job boards are quiet. What does a typical rejection actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly they say we've gone with a candidate with more experience. How do I get experience if nobody lets me in? Last week one firm told me a thousand people applied for four places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for how few openings there are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms, mainly, and the government that lets them. The firms shrank their graduate intake and then said there's a skills shortage. I'd like rules that make big firms train people, and I'd happily join a union of junior staff if one existed in my field.

say: The robots aren't the problem here, **firms** cutting their graduate intake is.
I'd say a plateau means hiring should **recover** eventually, so the wait is on them.
think: I'm still **stuck**, with 41,000 in debt and under a month saved.
Few firms nearby hire trainees, so **location** hurts more than any technology.
do: Send about **ten** applications a week, widening to charities and the public sector.
Ask the housing trust about **temporary** cover roles that could turn permanent.
Keep the three garden centre shifts and only travel to the **best** interviews.
feel: Tired and **heavy**, more from the debt and silence than from AI.
S0.quote: The firms shrank their graduate intake and then said there's a skills shortage. I'd like rules that make big firms train people
fieldNote: Blames **firms** and the state, not technology, in line with her outlook.
Calm about AI itself but pressured by **debt**, rent and the lack of nearby trainee jobs.
Mentions a junior-staff **union** unprompted, so collective action is a live idea.

steps.text: Send ten applications a week to firms, charities and councils
Ask the housing trust about temporary finance cover roles
Keep three garden centre shifts and skip low-odds interview trips
Keep the current routine and the shared room on Mill Road

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the junior jobs that vanish first, and that's exactly the door I'm trying to get through. At work and online I'd point out that firms call it efficiency but it means fewer trainees. Someone should be making the case for public support while people change jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm in the worst spot, because the checking, reconciling and data entry I did as an intern is the work software takes first. My internship supervisor at the audit firm said the team of six juniors was now four. I never learned the AI tools, so I'd be behind as well as unemployed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally make myself try one of these assistants, even though I hate the idea, because a recruiter told me not knowing them was a red flag. I'd also look at roles that need a person in the room, like helping tenants with money problems at the housing trust. I'd ask the careers service about a conversion course in tax advice and give it six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and a bit angry. I worked really hard for the grades and it feels like the ladder is being taken away while I'm still on the bottom rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI tools. Which part of an accountant's day do you think goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bank reconciliations, expense checks, the monthly ledger. I did the bank reconciliations by hand for ten weeks as an intern and a program does them in minutes. The judgement part, explaining a number to a worried tenant, stays human for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya (your housemate) if she asked whether to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya to learn the tools before she needs them, which is funny coming from me. Then I'd tell her to join anything collective, a union or a professional group, because one person alone can't bargain with a firm.

say: Firms call it **efficiency**, but it means fewer trainees and a cut ladder.
Government should provide **public support** while people change jobs.
think: The checking and reconciling I did as an intern is the work **software** takes first.
I never learned the tools, so I'd be **behind** and unemployed.
do: Try an **AI assistant** within the month, even though I dislike the idea.
Look at people-facing roles, like money advice for **tenants** at the housing trust.
Ask the careers service about a six-month **tax advice** course.
feel: **Scared** and angry that the bottom rung is disappearing.
S1.quote: I did the bank reconciliations by hand for ten weeks as an intern and a program does them in minutes.
fieldNote: Strong sense of **injustice**, but she admits her own gap: she has never used the tools.
Intern experience gives concrete detail on what exactly gets **automated**.
Turns to **people-facing** work and group solidarity as her fallback.

steps.text: Try an AI assistant on a sample ledger within the month
Ask the careers service about a six-month tax advice course
Join a young accountants' union or professional network
Apply for tenant money-advice roles at housing trusts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that nobody is prepared, not the government, not the firms, not families like mine. At friends' tables I'd be asking who pays for the debts when the jobs go. Online I'd back any demand for a basic income and a freeze on loan repayments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my degree turns into a very expensive receipt. Everything I trained for is thinking work, and that's the part that arrives in 2028 while I'm still paying off the loan. I'd have maybe a year before the entry-level jobs simply stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd call the loan company and ask to pause payments, and I'd write to my local representative. Then I'd try to get work that needs hands, like care work or the garden centre full-time, because robots for that come three years later. I'd also look for an even cheaper room, maybe in a cheaper town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panic, really, but quiet panic. It's like standing on a pier and watching the tide go out too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very little time. What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum cleans at a primary school and my dad's disabled, so there's no help there. I'd turn to the union, the church food bank if I had to, and Priya. Politicians, only as a way of pressing for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a lot of graduates would protest and I'd go to the marches. Alone I can't do much, but a thousand of us unpaid, in debt and in the street is a different matter.

say: Nobody is **prepared**, not firms, not government, not families like mine.
I'd back a **basic income** and a pause on loan repayments.
think: My degree becomes an expensive **receipt** when the thinking work goes in 2028.
I'd have maybe a **year** before entry-level jobs simply stop.
do: Call the loan company in the first month and ask to **pause** payments.
Write to my local representative and join **marches** with other graduates.
Take **full-time** hands-on work at the garden centre or in care.
feel: Quiet **panic**, like watching the tide go out too fast.
S2.quote: Everything I trained for is thinking work, and that's the part that arrives in 2028 while I'm still paying off the loan.
fieldNote: Turns to **collective** and political action, consistent with her views and thin family money.
Looks to **hands-on** work as a three-year shelter, reading the card correctly.
Fear is high but not **paralysed**; she has specific first-month steps.

steps.text: Call the loan company and ask to pause repayments
Write to my local representative about loan relief
Go to graduate marches and join a debt campaign
Take full-time garden centre or care work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning that nobody should ignore. With five years governments can write rules, and I'd press for them to make firms keep training people. I wouldn't be telling friends to panic, I'd be telling them to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still frightened, but there's room to try. I might get one proper job in accounting before 2031, and that's worth a lot because experience counts for something. The hard bit is the debt, since it doesn't care what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying for accounting jobs now, because a firm that hires me in 2027 gives me four years of experience before the thinking work is automated. I'd save everything I can from the garden centre and the first salary and pay down the loan hard. I'd also join the union of the first firm that hires me and go to the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more hopeful than the two year one, honestly. I can picture a plan, and a plan makes the fear smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years sounds a lot longer to you than two. What does it change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I got an entry-level salary I'd live on half of it, and push the rest at the loan, maybe 600 a month. That would be about 24,000 over four years, less than half. The rest I'd hope the state writes off if the economy changes that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay down the debt in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the state would have to forgive some of it. If everything we trained for stops being worth something by 2031, they can't expect us to keep paying as if nothing happened.

say: Five years is enough for governments to write **rules** that make firms keep training.
I'd tell friends not to panic but to **organise**.
think: There's room to try, and one proper accounting job before 2031 is worth a lot of **experience**.
The **debt** is the hard part because it ignores what's coming.
do: Keep applying now, since a hire in 2027 gives about four years of **experience**.
Save hard and put around **600** a month at the loan from a first salary.
Join the union at the first firm that hires me and go to **meetings**.
feel: A little more **hopeful**, since a plan makes the fear smaller.
S3.quote: A firm that hires me in 2027 gives me four years of experience before the thinking work is automated.
fieldNote: Time lets her convert fear into a **sequence**: job, experience, loan payments.
Still expects the state to write off part of the **debt**, a clear political expectation.
Mood drops from alarmed because she can picture a **path**, not because the risk is smaller.

steps.text: Keep applying to accounting firms so a 2027 hire is possible
Put around 600 a month at the student loan from a first salary
Join the union at the first firm and attend meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that ten years is generous and we should use it well. Schools and colleges should be teaching people what's coming, and firms should have to plan. I'd talk about it as a long project rather than an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel safer, but not safe. I'd be 33 by then, and I could build a whole career in accounting and still be pushed out in my thirties. I also see that ten years lets me clear the debt, which matters more to me than anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first accounting job I could get, qualify as a chartered accountant over three years, and clear the loan by the end of it. In parallel I'd spend a few evenings a month learning the AI tools, since I'm told I can't avoid that. I'd keep an eye on moving toward advisory work, the sort that involves sitting with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. It's the one I could plan around. I'd still wake some nights thinking about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, you could even change direction. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might change direction, yes. Qualifying gives me a credential that holds a bit longer, and then I'd move into advice work with people, like debt counselling, where I can see a person on the other side of the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who tells you to just wait it out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say waiting isn't free. People who waited in the last big change lost their jobs first. I'd rather be the one who prepared even if I resent it.

say: Ten years is **generous**, so schools and firms should plan for it properly.
I'd call it a long **project**, not an emergency.
think: I feel safer but not **safe**, since I'd be only 33 by 2036.
Ten years lets me clear the **debt**, which matters most.
do: Take the first **accounting** job and qualify as a chartered accountant over three years.
Spend a few evenings a month learning **AI tools**, however much I resent it.
Move toward **advice** work with people, such as debt counselling.
feel: Fairly **steady**, though the loan still wakes me some nights.
S4.quote: Waiting isn't free. People who waited in the last big change lost their jobs first.
fieldNote: Only scenario where she expects to hold a **job**; debt remains the main weight.
Even with time, she plans for work that keeps a **human** face to it.
Reluctant about the **tools** but accepts she needs them.

steps.text: Take the first accounting job offered and start the chartered exams
Qualify as a chartered accountant over three years
Learn an AI assistant two evenings a month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one, by a long way. Everything is too fast for someone with my debt and no one to fall back on. What would help is a pause on the loan repayments, a real graduate scheme that firms must run, and a union that speaks for people at the start of their careers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't lazy and we aren't whining. We did what we were told, worked hard and got the top results, and we'd like a fair chance at the work.

headlineQuote: We did what we were told, worked hard and got the top results, and we'd like a fair chance at the work.
portrait: Wendy is 23, top of her accounting class, with **41,000** in student debt and four months of silence from employers.
She shares a rented room, works garden centre shifts and has no family money to lean on.
She blames firms and the state rather than technology, and would join a **union** or a march.
She has never used AI tools and resents needing them, which makes the desk-work scenarios hit her hardest.
biggestWorry: The **2028** AGI scenario, because her debt and thin savings leave no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A **pause** on loan repayments, firms required to run graduate schemes, and a union for people starting their careers.
